items.questionText: Which word from the poem is an example of onomatopoeia (a word that copies the sound it describes)? A) roof   B) splash   C) clouds
items.answerKey: splash
stepByStepSolution: Onomatopoeia words sound like the noise they describe.
Look for a word that sounds like the action, like water moving.
"Splash" sounds like water hitting something, so it is onomatopoeia.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any noun connected to weather is onomatopoeia
Choosing a word just because it appears near an exclamation
hints: Look for a word that sounds like the noise it is describing.
It's the word about water hitting something — it starts with 'spl'.

items.answerKey: Puddles pop and puddles plop

Look at the first sound of each important word in the line.
"Puddles" and "plop" both start with the "p" sound, so this line has alliteration.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking alliteration means the words rhyme instead of starting the same
Only checking the very first word of the line instead of comparing several words

items.questionText: What is the difference between rhyme and rhythm in a poem?
answerKey: rhyme is matching end sounds and rhythm is the beat or pattern of the poem
rhyme is about sounds matching at the end of lines, while rhythm is the pattern of beats when you read it aloud
stepByStepSolution: Rhyme is when words end with the same sound, like "cat" and "hat".
Rhythm is the beat or pattern you feel when the poem is read aloud.
A poem can have rhythm without rhyme, and rhyme also helps create rhythm.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking rhyme and rhythm mean exactly the same thing
Believing a poem needs rhyme to have any rhythm at all
hints: Think about matching sounds versus a musical beat.
One is about how words sound at the end of lines; the other is about the beat you clap to.

items.answerKey: Paying attention to facial expressions, actions and music
stepByStepSolution: Without words, a viewer must rely on other clues.
Facial expressions, actions and music all give hints about feelings.

Thinking skipping ahead gives the same understanding as watching in order
hints: Think about what a video without words still shows you.

together they tell the whole story; music alone or images alone can miss part of the meaning
stepByStepSolution: Multimedia texts combine more than one type of information.
Images might show an action, while music shows the feeling behind it.
Using both together gives a fuller, more accurate understanding than using just one.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming images alone always tell the complete story
Believing music is just background noise with no meaning
hints: Think about what each part (pictures and music) adds on its own.

items.questionText: Which sentence is a metaphor? A) The clouds looked like fluffy cotton wool.   B) The classroom was a zoo during recess.   C) The wind blew through the trees.
items.answerKey: The classroom was a zoo during recess.
stepByStepSolution: A metaphor says one thing IS another thing, without using "like" or "as".
Option A uses "looked like", which is a simile, not a metaphor.
Option B says the classroom "was a zoo", directly comparing without "like" or "as", so it is a metaphor.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing metaphors with similes because both are comparisons
Thinking any comparison sentence must be a metaphor
hints: Look for a sentence that says something IS something else, not 'like' or 'as'.
One option compares using 'like'; the correct one does not.

items.questionText: Which sentence uses personification (giving human qualities to something that is not human)? A) The dog ran across the yard.   B) The old house groaned and creaked in the wind.   C) The car was red and shiny.
items.answerKey: The old house groaned and creaked in the wind.
stepByStepSolution: Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things.
Houses cannot really "groan", which is something a person or animal does.
Giving the house this human-like sound makes this sentence personification.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any description of an object counts as personification
Missing that 'groaned' is normally something living things do
hints: Think about which sentence gives a human-like action to a thing.
Houses don't really make sounds like people do — that's the clue.

items.questionText: In the sentence 'Time is money', what two things are being compared?
answerKey: time and money
time is compared to money
stepByStepSolution: A metaphor directly compares two things by saying one IS the other.
In this sentence, "time" is being compared to "money".
So the two things compared are time and money.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the sentence is literally saying time can be spent like coins
Naming only one of the two things being compared
hints: Look at the two nouns on either side of the word 'is'.
The sentence compares something you can't hold (time) to something you can (money).

items.questionText: Which sentence is an example of personification? A) The stars twinkled brightly in the sky.   B) The stars danced and winked at the sleepy town below.   C) The sky was full of stars.
items.answerKey: The stars danced and winked at the sleepy town below.
stepByStepSolution: Dancing and winking are actions that people do, not stars.
Giving the stars these human actions makes this personification.
The other options simply describe the stars without giving them human behaviour.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any lively description automatically counts as personification
Confusing vivid adjectives with giving something human actions
hints: Look for actions that only people or animals usually do.
'Danced' and 'winked' are human actions given to the stars.

items.questionText: Rewrite this plain sentence using personification: 'The wind blew hard.'
answerKey: the wind howled angrily
the wind roared through the trees
the wind whispered through the branches
the wind screamed across the field
stepByStepSolution: Personification gives a non-human thing human actions or feelings.
Think of an action a person or animal does when angry or loud, like howling or screaming.
Use that action to describe the wind, for example "the wind howled angrily".
commonMisconceptions: Simply adding an adjective, like 'the wind blew very hard', without adding a human action
Forgetting to give the wind an action a person or animal would actually do
hints: Think of a sound or action an angry person or animal might make.
Try using a word like 'howled', 'roared' or 'screamed' instead of 'blew'.

items.questionText: What is the effect of using the metaphor 'Her smile was sunshine' instead of saying 'Her smile was nice'? A) It gives no extra meaning at all.   B) It makes the smile feel warm, bright and comforting.   C) It makes the sentence harder to understand for no reason.
items.answerKey: It makes the smile feel warm, bright and comforting.
stepByStepSolution: A metaphor connects one thing to another that shares similar qualities.
Sunshine is warm and bright, so comparing a smile to it suggests those same qualities.
This makes the description feel much warmer and more vivid than simply saying "nice".
commonMisconceptions: Thinking metaphors only make writing more confusing
Missing the shared qualities between the two things being compared
hints: Think about the qualities of sunshine — what is it like?
Sunshine is warm and bright, so a smile compared to it feels the same way.

items.questionText: Which sentence combines BOTH personification and vivid description, rather than just one? A) The moon smiled down on the quiet, sleeping town.   B) The moon was bright and round in the sky.   C) The moon rose over the hills.
items.answerKey: The moon smiled down on the quiet, sleeping town.
stepByStepSolution: Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things.
"Smiled" is a human action given to the moon, and "sleeping town" also gives the town a human-like quality.
This sentence uses personification in two places, making it richer than the other options.
commonMisconceptions: Counting only obvious action words and missing personification in descriptive phrases like 'sleeping town'
Choosing an option simply because it sounds descriptive, without checking for human qualities
hints: Look for more than one place where something non-human is given human qualities.
Check both the moon's action and how the town is described.

items.questionText: Explain why a writer might choose the metaphor 'The classroom was a beehive' instead of saying 'The classroom was busy and noisy.'
answerKey: it creates a stronger, more vivid picture in the reader's mind by comparing the busy noise to a beehive full of buzzing bees
a beehive suggests lots of movement and buzzing, giving a clearer, more interesting picture than just saying busy and noisy
stepByStepSolution: Think about what a beehive is usually like — full of movement, buzzing and activity.
Comparing the classroom to a beehive lets the reader picture and almost hear that busy activity.
This creates a more vivid, memorable image than the plain description "busy and noisy".
commonMisconceptions: Thinking metaphors are only used to make sentences shorter
Not connecting the qualities of a beehive to the meaning of the metaphor
hints: Think about what a real beehive looks and sounds like.
The comparison helps the reader imagine buzzing activity, not just noise.

items.questionText: Which sentence is NOT an example of figurative language (it is meant literally)? A) The waves danced across the ocean.   B) The waves crashed onto the rocks and sprayed water everywhere.   C) The ocean was a wild, roaring beast.
items.answerKey: The waves crashed onto the rocks and sprayed water everywhere.
stepByStepSolution: Figurative language describes things in a way that is not literally true.
Waves crashing and spraying water can literally happen, so this sentence is meant literally.
The other two sentences give human or animal-like qualities to the waves and ocean, so they are figurative.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any exciting or dramatic sentence must be figurative
Missing that some strong verbs, like 'crashed', can still be literally true
hints: Ask yourself: could this actually happen exactly as described?
One sentence describes something waves can really and truly do.

items.questionText: What is the difference between a metaphor and personification?
answerKey: a metaphor compares two different things by saying one is the other, while personification gives human qualities to something that is not human
a metaphor says something is something else, while personification specifically gives human actions or feelings to non-human things
stepByStepSolution: A metaphor compares two different things directly, saying one thing "is" another.
Personification is a special kind of comparison that gives human actions or feelings to non-human things.
So personification is really a type of comparison focused only on human-like qualities, while metaphors can compare anything.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking metaphor and personification are exactly the same technique
Believing personification must always use the word 'is', like a metaphor does

hints: Think about whether the second sentence is a result of the first.

items.questionText: Give an example of a cohesive tie (linking word or phrase) that shows a contrast between two ideas.
answerKey: however
but
on the other hand
although
yet
stepByStepSolution: A contrast linking word shows that two ideas are different or opposite.
Words like "however" or "but" signal that the next idea will be different from the first.
Any of these words can correctly link two contrasting ideas.
commonMisconceptions: Giving a word that shows agreement (like 'also') instead of contrast
Confusing a time-order word (like 'then') with a contrast word
hints: Think of a word you use when two ideas don't agree.
A common example starts with the letter 'h' or 'b'.

items.questionText: Which sentence is a rhetorical question, often used in persuasive writing? A) The sky is blue today.   B) Don't you want your school to have a better playground?   C) The playground has three slides.
items.answerKey: Don't you want your school to have a better playground?
stepByStepSolution: A rhetorical question is asked to make the reader think, not to get a real answer.
It usually starts with words like "Don't you" or "Wouldn't it be great if".
Option B is phrased as a question designed to persuade, not to gather information.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any question in a text is automatically persuasive
Confusing a simple factual statement with a rhetorical question
hints: Look for a sentence that ends with a question mark.
This question is designed to make the reader agree, not to find out new information.

items.questionText: Which phrase uses emotive language (words chosen to create strong feelings)? A) The dog was in the yard.   B) The poor, frightened puppy shivered alone in the cold.   C) The dog is brown and white.
items.answerKey: The poor, frightened puppy shivered alone in the cold.
stepByStepSolution: Emotive language uses words that create strong feelings, like sadness or sympathy.
Words like "poor", "frightened" and "shivered alone" are chosen to make the reader feel sorry for the puppy.
The other options are plain, factual descriptions with no strong feeling attached.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any description with adjectives is automatically emotive
Missing that plain colour descriptions do not usually create strong feelings
hints: Look for words designed to make you feel sorry or upset.
This option is written to tug at your heartstrings.

items.questionText: Name one persuasive device a writer might use to convince readers to agree with their opinion.
answerKey: rhetorical question
emotive language
repetition
stepByStepSolution: Persuasive writing often uses special techniques to convince readers.
Common devices include rhetorical questions, emotive language and repetition.
Naming any one of these is a correct persuasive device.
commonMisconceptions: Naming a device used in stories, like personification, instead of a persuasive device
Describing a fact instead of naming a technique
hints: Think about techniques used in advertisements or opinion pieces.
One example starts with the letter 'r' (two of them do!).

items.questionText: Which sentence uses repetition as a persuasive device? A) Recycling helps the planet. Recycling saves resources. Recycling is something we can all do.   B) Recycling is good for many reasons.   C) We should recycle more often at school.
items.answerKey: Recycling helps the planet. Recycling saves resources. Recycling is something we can all do.
stepByStepSolution: Repetition means using the same word or phrase multiple times for effect.
In option A, the word "Recycling" is repeated at the start of each sentence.
This repeated pattern makes the message feel stronger and easier to remember.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any mention of the topic word counts as repetition, even without a repeated pattern
Missing that repetition usually needs the SAME word or phrase used more than once for effect
hints: Look for a word that appears at the start of several sentences.
Count how many times the word 'Recycling' appears.

items.questionText: Why do persuasive writers use emotive language instead of plain facts?
answerKey: to make the reader feel strong emotions, which can make them more likely to agree with the writer's opinion
emotive words create feelings like sympathy or excitement, which can convince readers to support the writer's point of view
stepByStepSolution: Emotive language is designed to create strong feelings in the reader.
Strong feelings, like sympathy or excitement, can make a reader more likely to agree with an opinion.
This is why persuasive writers often choose emotive words over plain, neutral facts.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking emotive language is used only to make writing longer
Believing facts alone are always more persuasive than feelings
hints: Think about how feelings can influence a person's opinion.
Emotive words are chosen on purpose to affect the reader's emotions.

items.questionText: Which rhetorical question would best suit a persuasive text arguing that students should have more time for reading? A) What is your favourite book?   B) Wouldn't it be wonderful if every student had time to enjoy a great book each day?   C) How many pages are in your book?
items.answerKey: Wouldn't it be wonderful if every student had time to enjoy a great book each day?
stepByStepSolution: A persuasive rhetorical question should support the writer's argument, not just ask for information.
Option B is designed to make the reader agree that more reading time would be wonderful.
The other questions simply ask for facts and do not push the reader toward an opinion.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing a genuine information-seeking question instead of a persuasive one
Not connecting the question back to the specific argument about reading time
hints: Look for the question that pushes the reader toward agreeing with an opinion.
The correct question is not really asking for information.

items.questionText: A persuasive text about keeping classrooms tidy says: 'A tidy classroom is a happy classroom. A tidy classroom helps us learn. A tidy classroom makes us proud.' Identify the persuasive device used and explain its effect.
answerKey: repetition of 'a tidy classroom' at the start of each sentence, which makes the message memorable and emphasises the idea strongly
the device is repetition; repeating the same phrase makes the argument stick in the reader's mind and feel more convincing
stepByStepSolution: Notice that the phrase "A tidy classroom" is repeated at the start of each sentence.
This repeated structure is the persuasive device called repetition.
Repetition makes the idea more memorable and gives the argument a stronger, more convincing rhythm.
commonMisconceptions: Naming the device correctly but not explaining its effect on the reader
Confusing repetition with alliteration, since both involve repeated elements
hints: Look at what phrase is repeated at the beginning of each sentence.
Think about why repeating a phrase makes an argument feel stronger.

items.questionText: Which combination of persuasive devices is used in this sentence? 'Don't you care about our poor, suffering planet? We must act now, now, now!' A) Rhetorical question and repetition only   B) Rhetorical question, emotive language and repetition   C) Emotive language only
items.answerKey: Rhetorical question, emotive language and repetition
stepByStepSolution: Identify the question at the start — this is a rhetorical question.
Notice emotional words like "poor, suffering" — this is emotive language.
Notice "now, now, now" repeated three times — this is repetition, so all three devices are used together.
commonMisconceptions: Missing one of the three devices because they appear together in the same sentence
Confusing emotive language with repetition when both appear close together
hints: Check for a question, feeling-words, AND a repeated word, all in this one sentence.
There are three different persuasive devices working together here.

items.questionText: Why might a persuasive text combine several devices, like a rhetorical question AND emotive language, rather than using just one? A) To make the writing longer without any real purpose.   B) To make the argument feel more powerful and convincing from multiple angles.   C) Combining devices actually weakens persuasive writing.
items.answerKey: To make the argument feel more powerful and convincing from multiple angles.
stepByStepSolution: Each persuasive device works on the reader in a slightly different way.
Using several together — like making the reader think AND feel — can strengthen an argument.
This combination makes the overall message more powerful and convincing than using just one device.
commonMisconceptions: Believing that using more devices simply makes a text longer with no extra effect
Thinking combining techniques makes an argument confusing rather than stronger
hints: Think about how a question and a feeling might work together.
Using more than one technique can affect the reader in more than one way.

items.questionText: What is emotive language?
answerKey: language chosen to create strong feelings in the reader
words that make the reader feel a strong emotion, like sadness, excitement or anger
stepByStepSolution: Think about the word "emotive", which relates to emotions.
Emotive language is made up of words chosen to create strong feelings in the reader.
It is often used in persuasive writing to influence how the reader feels about a topic.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing emotive language with simply using long or difficult words
Thinking emotive language must always be sad, when it can also be excited or angry
hints: Think about the word 'emotion' hidden inside 'emotive'.
It's about words chosen to make you FEEL something.

items.questionText: You are reading and a sentence doesn't make sense. What is a good self-correction strategy to try first? A) Skip the rest of the book.   B) Reread the sentence carefully.   C) Close the book and stop reading.
items.answerKey: Reread the sentence carefully.
stepByStepSolution: Self-correction strategies help readers fix confusion while reading.
Rereading a confusing sentence often helps you notice a missed word or detail.
This is usually the first and simplest strategy to try when something doesn't make sense.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking giving up on a confusing text is an acceptable first response
Believing skipping ahead always solves confusion, rather than checking the sentence again
hints: Think of the simplest thing you could do before trying anything else.
Going back over the same words again can help.

items.questionText: You read an unfamiliar word and are not sure what it means. What can you check to help work out its meaning? A) The words and sentences around it (the context)   B) The colour of the book cover   C) How many pages are left
items.answerKey: The words and sentences around it (the context)
stepByStepSolution: Context clues are the words and sentences surrounding an unfamiliar word.
These surrounding words often give hints about what the unfamiliar word means.
Checking the context is a reliable way to work out an unknown word's meaning.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking unrelated details, like the book cover, could help with word meaning
Assuming an unfamiliar word must be looked up immediately rather than using context first
hints: Think about the words that appear just before and after the tricky word.
This strategy is called using 'context clues'.

items.questionText: Name one thing a reader should ask themselves to check they understand what they just read.
answerKey: does this make sense
did that make sense to me
what just happened in the story
stepByStepSolution: Good readers regularly check their own understanding.
A useful question to ask is simply, "Does this make sense?"
Asking this helps a reader notice quickly if they need to reread or fix something.
commonMisconceptions: Suggesting a question unrelated to comprehension, like asking about the author's name
Thinking self-checking questions are only needed at the very end of a whole book
hints: Think of a short question you could ask yourself while reading.
It's about whether the text makes sense to you.

items.questionText: A student reads: 'The dog chase the ball' and notices it sounds wrong. What self-correction strategy would help fix this? A) Rereading the sentence and checking if the grammar sounds right   B) Ignoring it and reading the next sentence   C) Closing the book
items.answerKey: Rereading the sentence and checking if the grammar sounds right
stepByStepSolution: Noticing a sentence "sounds wrong" is a sign to use self-correction.
Rereading the sentence lets the reader check whether the grammar and meaning make sense.
In this case, rereading would help notice "chase" should be "chased".
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring the mistake instead of pausing to fix understanding
Believing self-correction only applies to whole sentences making sense, not grammar
hints: Think about what happens when you say a sentence with an error out loud.
Go back and check it against how the sentence should sound.

items.questionText: Explain why using context clues is a helpful self-correction strategy when reading an unfamiliar word.
answerKey: because the surrounding words can give hints about the meaning, helping the reader keep understanding the text without stopping to look everything up
context clues let you guess a reasonable meaning from nearby words, so you can keep reading and understanding smoothly
stepByStepSolution: Context clues come from the words and sentences around an unfamiliar word.
These clues often hint at what the unfamiliar word probably means.
Using context lets a reader keep understanding the text without stopping to look up every word.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking context clues always give the exact dictionary meaning, rather than just a reasonable guess
Believing this strategy only works for very easy words
hints: Think about how nearby words can hint at meaning.
This strategy helps you keep reading smoothly.

items.questionText: Which situation shows a reader correctly using self-correction? A) Maya reads a sentence, notices it doesn't make sense, and rereads it to fix her understanding.   B) Liam skips every hard word without trying to work it out.   C) Priya closes the book whenever she meets a tricky sentence.
items.answerKey: Maya reads a sentence, notices it doesn't make sense, and rereads it to fix her understanding.
stepByStepSolution: Self-correction means noticing confusion and taking action to fix it.
Maya notices the sentence is confusing and takes the useful step of rereading it.
This shows an active attempt to fix understanding, unlike simply skipping or giving up.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any pause while reading counts as self-correction, even without action to fix it
Confusing avoidance (skipping, stopping) with an actual correction strategy
hints: Look for the reader who takes an active step to fix their confusion.
The other two readers avoid the problem instead of solving it.

items.questionText: Describe two different self-correction strategies a reader could use if they got confused midway through a tricky paragraph.
answerKey: rereading the paragraph and using context clues to work out any unfamiliar words
checking whether the sentence makes sense and rereading it, or looking at surrounding words for clues to a tricky word's meaning
stepByStepSolution: Self-correction strategies include several different actions a reader can take.
One strategy is rereading the confusing part carefully.
Another strategy is using context clues from nearby words to work out anything unfamiliar.
commonMisconceptions: Naming the same strategy twice with different wording instead of two distinct strategies
Suggesting giving up as one of the 'strategies'
hints: Think of one strategy about going back over text, and one about word meaning.
Rereading is one; using nearby words for clues is another.

items.questionText: A reader reaches the end of a page and realises they cannot remember what happened. What is the BEST self-correction strategy? A) Keep reading forward and hope it becomes clear later.   B) Go back and reread the page, checking understanding as they go.   C) Skip to the very last page of the book.
items.answerKey: Go back and reread the page, checking understanding as they go.
stepByStepSolution: Forgetting what happened is a clear sign of lost understanding.
The best fix is to go back and reread, checking understanding along the way.
Continuing forward without fixing this gap would likely cause more confusion later.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming confusion will simply resolve itself if the reader keeps going
Thinking skipping to the end could ever fix a comprehension gap in the middle of the text
hints: Think about what happens if you keep reading without fixing your understanding.
Going backwards, not forwards, solves this problem.

items.questionText: Why is it important for a reader to notice when a sentence 'doesn't sound right', rather than just continuing to read?
answerKey: because noticing this helps the reader catch a misunderstanding or mistake early, before it affects their understanding of the rest of the text
if a reader ignores a sentence that sounds wrong, confusion can build up and make the rest of the text harder to understand
stepByStepSolution: A sentence that "doesn't sound right" is often a sign of a misread word or a misunderstanding.
Noticing this early lets the reader fix the issue before it causes more confusion.
If ignored, small misunderstandings can build up and make the rest of the text much harder to follow.
commonMisconceptions: Believing one small missed detail never affects later understanding
Thinking self-correction is only useful for very long texts, not shorter ones
hints: Think about what could happen if small mistakes are never fixed.
Catching problems early stops them from growing bigger.

items.questionText: Which of these is an example of 'checking it makes sense' while reading? A) Counting how many words are on the page.   B) Pausing to ask yourself if what you just read fits with the rest of the story.   C) Looking at the pictures only, without reading the words.
items.answerKey: Pausing to ask yourself if what you just read fits with the rest of the story.
stepByStepSolution: "Checking it makes sense" means monitoring your own understanding as you read.
This involves pausing to think about whether the text fits with what came before.
The other options do not involve checking understanding of the meaning at all.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing checking for meaning with checking surface features like word count
Thinking looking only at pictures is the same as checking whether the text makes sense
hints: Think about what 'making sense' really means when reading.
The correct answer involves thinking about the story's meaning.

items.questionText: Which sentence uses direct speech (the exact words someone said, in quotation marks)? A) Sam said that he was hungry.   B) Sam said, "I am hungry."   C) Sam told his mum he wanted food.
items.answerKey: Sam said, "I am hungry."
stepByStepSolution: Direct speech shows a person's exact words inside quotation marks.
Option B has quotation marks around Sam's exact words, "I am hungry."
The other options describe what Sam said without using his exact words or quotation marks.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any sentence with the word 'said' is automatically direct speech
Missing the quotation marks as the key sign of direct speech
hints: Look for the sentence with quotation marks.
Direct speech shows the exact words a person used.

items.questionText: Convert this direct speech into reported speech: Mia said, "I am tired."
answerKey: Mia said that she was tired.
Mia said she was tired.
stepByStepSolution: Remove the quotation marks; adding the word "that" is optional.
Change "I am" to "she was" because we are now reporting, not quoting directly.
The reported speech becomes "Mia said (that) she was tired."
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to change the pronoun 'I' to 'she'
Forgetting to change the tense from 'am' to 'was'
hints: Change 'I' to the correct pronoun for Mia.
Change 'am' to the past tense form 'was'.

items.questionText: Which sentence is written in reported (indirect) speech? A) Jack shouted, "Watch out!"   B) Jack shouted that everyone should watch out.   C) "Watch out!" shouted Jack.
items.answerKey: Jack shouted that everyone should watch out.
stepByStepSolution: Reported speech tells us what someone said without using their exact words or quotation marks.
Option B reports what Jack said using the word "that", with no quotation marks.
The other two options use quotation marks, so they are direct speech.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking direct speech with the quote at the start of the sentence is reported speech
Confusing reported speech with direct speech simply because both mention what was said
hints: Look for the sentence with no quotation marks.
Reported speech usually uses the word 'that'.

items.questionText: Convert this reported speech into direct speech, using correct punctuation: Ben said that he loved pizza.
answerKey: Ben said, "I love pizza."
Ben said, "I love pizza".
stepByStepSolution: Change "he loved" back to the exact words Ben would have said, "I love".
Add quotation marks around the exact words.
The direct speech becomes: Ben said, "I love pizza."
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to add quotation marks around the exact words
Forgetting to change 'he' back to 'I' and 'loved' back to 'love'
hints: Change the pronoun and tense back to how Ben would have said it himself.
Don't forget the quotation marks.

items.questionText: When changing direct speech to reported speech, what usually happens to the verb tense? A) It stays exactly the same.   B) It often shifts back into the past tense.   C) It always changes into a question.
items.answerKey: It often shifts back into the past tense.
stepByStepSolution: In reported speech, we are usually retelling something that was said earlier.
Because of this, the verb often shifts back one step into the past tense, for example "am" becomes "was".
This tense shift is a key rule when converting direct speech into reported speech.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming reported speech keeps the exact same tense as direct speech
Confusing reported speech with turning a sentence into a question
hints: Think about the example: 'I am tired' becomes 'she was tired'.
The tense usually moves one step into the past.

items.questionText: Convert this direct speech into reported speech: The teacher said, "You are all doing a great job."
answerKey: The teacher said that they were all doing a great job.
The teacher said everyone was doing a great job.
The teacher said that we were all doing a great job.
stepByStepSolution: Remove the quotation marks from the exact words.
Change "You are" to a reported form, such as "they were" or "everyone was".
Combine this into a full reported sentence: "The teacher said that they were all doing a great job."
commonMisconceptions: Leaving 'you' unchanged instead of switching to an appropriate pronoun
Forgetting to shift 'are' into the past tense 'were'
hints: Change 'you' to a word like 'they' or 'everyone'.
Change 'are' to 'were'.

items.questionText: Which sentence correctly converts 'Lily said, "I will finish my homework tonight."' into reported speech? A) Lily said that I will finish my homework tonight.   B) Lily said that she would finish her homework that night.   C) Lily said, she would finish her homework tonight.
items.answerKey: Lily said that she would finish her homework that night.
stepByStepSolution: Change the pronoun "I" to "she" because we are reporting about Lily.
Change "will" to "would" and "my" to "her" to match reported speech rules.
Also change "tonight" to "that night" since we are now retelling this at a later time — this matches option B.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to change more than one word, such as only fixing the pronoun but not the verb
Leaving quotation marks in what should be a fully reported sentence
hints: More than one word needs to change: the pronoun, the verb, and the time word.
Check 'will' and 'tonight' as well as 'I' and 'my'.

items.questionText: Explain why we usually change words like 'I', 'my' and 'tonight' when converting direct speech into reported speech.
answerKey: because reported speech is retold from a different point of view, often later, so pronouns and time words need to change to still make sense
the pronouns and time words need to match who is speaking now and when the sentence is being told, since it's no longer the exact quoted moment
stepByStepSolution: Direct speech shows the exact words at the exact moment they were said.
Reported speech retells this later, often from a different speaker's point of view.
Because of this shift, pronouns (like "I" to "she") and time words (like "tonight" to "that night") must change to still make sense.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking these words never need to change because the meaning is the same
Believing only pronouns need to change, forgetting time words also shift
hints: Think about who is speaking and when, in reported speech versus direct speech.
The change happens because we are retelling this from a new point of view, often later.

items.questionText: Which sentence has a mistake in converting speech, and what is it? 'Original: Dad said, "I am cooking dinner." Converted: Dad said that I am cooking dinner.' A) The mistake is a missing quotation mark.   B) The mistake is that the pronoun and tense were not changed correctly.   C) There is no mistake.
items.answerKey: The mistake is that the pronoun and tense were not changed correctly.
stepByStepSolution: In reported speech, "I" should usually change to "he" since we are talking about Dad.
"Am" should also usually shift to "was" to match reported speech rules.
The converted sentence kept "I am" unchanged, which is the mistake.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the mistake is about punctuation, when reported speech should not have quotation marks at all here
Not noticing that both the pronoun and the tense are still incorrect
hints: Compare the pronoun 'I' in the direct and reported versions.
Also compare the verb tense between 'am' and what it should become.

items.questionText: Which punctuation is needed around a person's exact spoken words in direct speech? A) Question marks   B) Quotation marks   C) Exclamation marks
items.answerKey: Quotation marks
stepByStepSolution: Direct speech shows someone's exact words.
These exact words are always placed inside quotation marks.
This is different from reported speech, which uses no quotation marks at all.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing quotation marks with exclamation marks, which show strong feeling instead
Thinking punctuation for direct speech depends on what is being said
hints: Think about the punctuation marks that look like little floating commas.
This punctuation always surrounds the exact spoken words.

items.questionText: How does Mia feel after coming last in the race? A) Proud and excited   B) Disappointed but determined to improve   C) Angry at her brother
items.answerKey: Disappointed but determined to improve
stepByStepSolution: Look at how Mia's disappointment is described — her cheeks "burned with disappointment".
Then notice what she does that evening — she makes a plan and asks for help.
This shows she feels disappointed but is determined to keep improving.
commonMisconceptions: Focusing only on her disappointment and missing her determined actions afterward
Assuming she is angry, when no anger is described in the passage
hints: Look at both her feelings AND her actions that evening.
Her actions show more than just her feelings — what does she plan to do?
items.passage:
Mia's Race

Mia trained every afternoon for the cross-country race, running a little further each week. On the day of the event, however, she came last, and her legs ached while her cheeks burned with disappointment. That evening, Mia wrote a list of three things she could practise before the next race and asked her older brother to jog with her on weekends.

items.questionText: How does Jake respond to coming last in the race? A) He makes a plan to train harder.   B) He gives up on running and avoids sport altogether.   C) He asks his coach for extra help.
items.answerKey: He gives up on running and avoids sport altogether.
stepByStepSolution: Look at Jake's actions after the race — he throws his shoes and declares he'll never race again.
He then avoids sport for the rest of the term.
This shows he responds by giving up, rather than trying to improve.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing Jake's reaction with Mia's, since both come last in a race
Assuming saying running is 'boring' means he simply lost interest, rather than seeing it as avoidance after disappointment
hints: Look at what Jake does with his running shoes.
Notice what he avoids doing for the rest of the term.
items.passage:
Jake's Race

Jake also came last in the cross-country race, after barely training at all. He kicked off his running shoes and threw them into the corner of his room, declaring that running was pointless and he would never race again. He avoided sport for the rest of the term, telling his friends that running was "boring anyway."

items.questionText: Mia and Jake face the same problem: coming last in a race. What is one key difference in how they respond?
answerKey: Mia makes a plan to improve and asks for help, while Jake gives up and avoids running altogether
Mia responds by trying to get better, but Jake responds by quitting and avoiding sport
stepByStepSolution: Identify what Mia does after the race — she plans and asks for help.
Identify what Jake does after the race — he gives up and avoids sport.
The key difference is that Mia responds with determination, while Jake responds by giving up.
commonMisconceptions: Only describing one character's response instead of comparing both
Saying they respond the same way because they both feel disappointed at first
hints: Think about what each character DOES after feeling disappointed.
One character makes a plan; the other avoids the problem.

items.questionText: Which word best describes Mia's attitude toward the setback of coming last? A) Resilient (able to recover and keep trying)   B) Careless   C) Frightened
items.answerKey: Resilient (able to recover and keep trying)
stepByStepSolution: Think about the meaning of "resilient" — bouncing back from a setback.
Mia feels disappointed but still makes a plan and asks for help to improve.
This shows she is resilient, recovering from the setback rather than giving up.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing feeling disappointed briefly with being careless or unaffected by the loss
Missing that resilience includes both feeling upset AND still trying again
hints: Think about a word that means 'bouncing back after a difficult moment'.
Mia feels upset, but what does she do next?

items.answerKey: Discouraged and avoidant
stepByStepSolution: Think about what Jake does after the race — he gives up and avoids sport.
This shows he feels discouraged and is avoiding the activity that upset him.
This is different from being resilient or confident, since he stops trying altogether.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing 'resilient' by mistake, confusing Jake's response with Mia's
Overlooking that avoiding something is a clear sign of feeling discouraged
hints: Think about what Jake avoids doing after the race.

items.questionText: Explain how Mia's and Jake's different responses might lead to different results in the FUTURE.
answerKey: Mia is likely to improve over time because she is practising and getting help, while Jake is unlikely to improve because he has given up and stopped training
because Mia keeps practising and Jake avoids running altogether, Mia will probably get better at racing while Jake probably won't improve

Chirping all night long, long, long.
The moon peeks out, round and bright,
Watching over my backyard at night.
Stars begin to twinkle and gleam,
Time to close my eyes and dream.

items.questionText: Which of these is a technique commonly used in poetry to create rhythm or emphasis? A) Repetition   B) A bibliography   C) A table of contents
items.answerKey: Repetition
stepByStepSolution: Poems often use special techniques to create rhythm and emphasis.
Repetition, or repeating words and phrases, is a common technique used for this purpose.
The other options are not poetry techniques at all.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing poetry techniques with parts of an information book, like a bibliography
Thinking any list of words counts as poetic technique
hints: Think about a technique involving repeating words.
The other two options are found in non-fiction books, not poems.

items.questionText: Name one reason a poet might choose to use rhyme in a poem.
answerKey: to make the poem sound musical or pleasing to hear
rhyme helps the poem flow and can make it more memorable or fun to read aloud
stepByStepSolution: Rhyme connects the ends of lines with matching sounds.
This can make a poem sound musical and pleasing when read aloud.
It can also make the poem more memorable and fun to read.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking rhyme is only used to make poems easier to write
Believing rhyme has no real effect on how a poem sounds or feels
hints: Think about how a poem sounds when it rhymes, compared to when it doesn't.
Rhyme can make a poem easier to remember and more enjoyable to hear.

items.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon to introduce a list? A) I need to buy: apples, bread and milk.   B) I need to buy the following items: apples, bread and milk.   C) I need to: buy apples, bread and milk.
items.answerKey: I need to buy the following items: apples, bread and milk.
stepByStepSolution: A colon introduces a list after a complete introductory statement.
"I need to buy the following items" is a complete sentence, so it can be followed by a colon and then the list.
The other options place the colon in the middle of an incomplete sentence, which is incorrect.
commonMisconceptions: Placing a colon directly after a verb, like 'buy:', instead of after a complete introductory phrase
Thinking any list needs a colon before it, even in a short simple sentence
hints: Check whether the words before the colon form a complete sentence on their own.
The colon should come after a full introductory statement, not in the middle of one.

items.questionText: Which word is the correct contraction for 'do not'? A) don't   B) dont   C) do'nt
items.answerKey: don't
stepByStepSolution: A contraction joins two words together and uses an apostrophe to show missing letters.
"Do not" becomes "don't", with the apostrophe replacing the missing "o" in "not".
The other options are missing the apostrophe or have it in the wrong place.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting the apostrophe altogether
Placing the apostrophe in the wrong position within the word
hints: Think about which letter is missing when 'do not' becomes one word.
The apostrophe should replace the missing letter, not be placed randomly.

items.questionText: Write the contraction for 'they are'.
answerKey: they're
stepByStepSolution: Contractions combine two words and use an apostrophe for missing letters.
"They are" combines into "they're", with the apostrophe replacing the missing "a".
So the correct contraction is "they're".
commonMisconceptions: Confusing 'they're' with 'their' or 'there', which sound the same but mean different things
Forgetting to include the apostrophe
hints: Think about which letter is missing from 'are' when it joins 'they'.
Be careful not to confuse this with the word 'their'.

items.questionText: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly to show something belongs to someone? A) The dogs bone was buried in the yard.   B) The dog's bone was buried in the yard.   C) The dog's are buried in the yard.
items.answerKey: The dog's bone was buried in the yard.
stepByStepSolution: An apostrophe can show that something belongs to someone (possession) as well as showing missing letters.
"The dog's bone" shows the bone belongs to the dog, using an apostrophe before the "s".
Option A is missing the apostrophe, and option C incorrectly uses an apostrophe with a plural word.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting the apostrophe when showing possession
Confusing a possessive apostrophe with a plural word ending in 's'
hints: Look for the sentence where the bone clearly belongs to the dog.
Check exactly where the apostrophe is placed.

items.questionText: When should a new paragraph usually begin in a piece of writing?
answerKey: when the topic or main idea changes
a new paragraph starts when you move on to a new idea, event or point
stepByStepSolution: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea.
When the writing moves on to a new idea, event or point, a new paragraph should begin.
This helps organise the writing so it is easier for the reader to follow.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a new paragraph should start after every single sentence
Believing paragraph breaks are based on length rather than a change in idea
hints: Think about what changes between one paragraph and the next.
It's about a shift in idea, not the number of sentences.

items.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon before a list? A) My favourite sports are: soccer, netball and swimming.   B) My favourite sports include the following: soccer, netball and swimming.   C) My favourite: sports are soccer, netball and swimming.
items.answerKey: My favourite sports include the following: soccer, netball and swimming.
stepByStepSolution: A colon should follow a complete sentence that introduces a list.
"My favourite sports include the following" is a complete sentence on its own.
Option A is a common mistake because "are:" does not form a complete introductory statement in the same way.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a colon can always follow the verb 'are' directly before a list
Placing the colon randomly in the middle of the sentence
hints: Check if the words before the colon make complete sense as their own sentence.
One option places the colon in an awkward, incorrect position.

items.questionText: Explain why writers use paragraphs when writing several ideas about a topic, instead of writing everything as one long block of text.
answerKey: paragraphs organise ideas into clear groups, making the writing easier for the reader to follow and understand
breaking writing into paragraphs helps separate different ideas so the reader is not confused by everything running together
stepByStepSolution: Think about how confusing it would be to read many different ideas with no breaks.
Paragraphs organise the writing by grouping similar ideas together.
This structure makes the text much easier for a reader to follow and understand.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking paragraphs are only used to make writing look neater, with no effect on meaning
Believing paragraph breaks are optional and don't affect a reader's understanding
hints: Think about how hard one giant block of text would be to read.
Paragraphs group similar ideas together for the reader.

items.questionText: Which sentence uses BOTH an apostrophe for a contraction AND a colon for a list correctly? A) I can't wait for the party: it's got games, cake and music.   B) I cant wait for the party: its got games, cake, and music.   C) I can't wait for the party, it's got games: cake and music.
items.answerKey: I can't wait for the party: it's got games, cake and music.
stepByStepSolution: Check the contractions first — "can't" and "it's" both need apostrophes.
Then check the colon — it should come after a complete introductory sentence, before the list.
Option A has both apostrophes correctly placed and the colon correctly introducing the list.
commonMisconceptions: Missing one of the two required apostrophes
Placing the colon in the wrong spot within the sentence, splitting the list incorrectly
hints: Check both apostrophes are present and correctly placed.
Check the colon comes right before the full list starts.

items.questionText: A student wrote one huge paragraph containing three completely different ideas: their weekend, their pet, and their favourite food. Explain what they should do to fix this.
answerKey: they should split the writing into three separate paragraphs, one for each idea
break the single paragraph into three paragraphs so each idea (weekend, pet, favourite food) has its own paragraph
stepByStepSolution: Notice that the paragraph actually contains three separate, unrelated ideas.
Each idea should have its own paragraph, since a paragraph should focus on one main idea.
The fix is to split the single paragraph into three separate paragraphs, one for each topic.
commonMisconceptions: Suggesting the paragraph just needs more punctuation, rather than being split into separate paragraphs
Thinking all three ideas can still be one paragraph as long as it's well written
hints: Count how many different ideas are packed into this one paragraph.
Each idea should get its own paragraph.

items.questionText: Which of these has a paragraphing mistake? A) A paragraph about pets, followed by a new paragraph about weekends.   B) One giant paragraph that talks about pets, then weekends, then favourite foods, all together.   C) A paragraph about pets, followed by a separate paragraph about favourite foods.
items.answerKey: One giant paragraph that talks about pets, then weekends, then favourite foods, all together.
stepByStepSolution: Check each option for whether ideas are properly separated into their own paragraphs.
Options A and C correctly separate different topics into their own paragraphs.
Option B crams three different topics into one giant paragraph, which is the mistake.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a longer paragraph is automatically better organised than several shorter ones
Not noticing that multiple unrelated topics have been squeezed into a single paragraph
hints: Count how many different topics are inside each option.
One option keeps everything in a single paragraph.

items.questionText: A poster about recycling has a picture of rubbish but text that talks about saving water. What is the main problem with this poster? A) The picture and text don't match or work together.   B) The poster has too many colours.   C) The poster is too short.
items.answerKey: The picture and text don't match or work together.
stepByStepSolution: In a multimodal text, the picture and words should work together to share one clear message.
Here, the picture is about rubbish/recycling, but the text is about saving water, which is a different topic.
This mismatch is the main problem, since the two parts should support the same message.
commonMisconceptions: Focusing on surface features like colour or length instead of checking if the message matches
Assuming any picture works as long as it looks interesting
hints: Check what message the picture shows compared to what the words say.
The two parts should be about the same topic.

items.questionText: What does 'multimodal text' mean?
answerKey: a text that uses more than one mode, like words and pictures, together to share a message
a text that combines pictures, words, and sometimes sound to communicate a message
stepByStepSolution: "Multi" means many, and "modal" relates to different modes or ways of communicating.
A multimodal text uses more than one way to share a message, such as words and pictures together.
Posters, picture books and videos are all examples of multimodal texts.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking multimodal only means a text with many pages
Confusing multimodal texts with texts that just have a lot of words
hints: Think about the word 'multi', meaning many.
It's about a text using more than one type of communication, like pictures and words.

items.questionText: A teacher gives feedback that a poster's words are too small to read from the back of the classroom. What is the BEST way to revise the poster based on this feedback? A) Add more pictures.   B) Make the text larger and clearer.   C) Change the poster's topic completely.
items.answerKey: Make the text larger and clearer.
stepByStepSolution: Feedback should be used to directly fix the specific problem mentioned.
The feedback is about the text being too small to read, not about the topic or pictures.
The best revision is to make the text larger and clearer, directly addressing the feedback given.
commonMisconceptions: Making an unrelated change, like adding pictures, instead of fixing the specific problem raised
Overreacting to feedback by changing something not mentioned at all, like the topic
hints: Focus only on the specific problem the feedback mentions.
The feedback is about the size of the text, not about pictures or topic.

items.questionText: Why is it important for the words and images in a poster to work together, rather than showing different, unrelated ideas?
answerKey: because if they don't match, the message becomes confusing and the reader may not understand what the poster is really about
when words and pictures don't match, the reader gets a confusing or mixed message instead of one clear idea
stepByStepSolution: A poster's job is to communicate one clear message to the reader.
If the words and pictures show different, unrelated ideas, the reader may become confused.
Making sure both parts work together helps the poster communicate its message clearly.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking pictures are just decoration and don't need to match the words
Believing a poster can have two unrelated messages as long as both look good
hints: Think about how a reader might feel if the words and picture don't match.
One clear message is easier for the reader to understand than two mixed ones.

items.questionText: A student's book cover shows a calm, sunny picture, but the story inside is a scary mystery. Based on this feedback, what change would improve the cover? A) Keep the same picture, since covers don't need to match the story.   B) Change the picture to something that hints at mystery or suspense, matching the story's mood.   C) Remove the picture completely and use only text.
items.answerKey: Change the picture to something that hints at mystery or suspense, matching the story's mood.
stepByStepSolution: A book cover should give readers a hint about the story's mood and content.
A calm, sunny picture does not match a scary mystery story.
The best revision is to change the picture so it reflects the mystery and suspense of the story.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming a book cover's image doesn't need to relate to the story's mood at all
Choosing an overly drastic fix, like removing the picture entirely, instead of matching it to the story
hints: Think about what a reader would expect from the cover before reading the story.
The picture should give a hint about the story's mood.

items.questionText: A classmate gives you this feedback on your poster: 'I like the picture, but I'm not sure what the poster is trying to tell me.' What specific part of your poster should you focus on improving?
answerKey: the words or message of the poster, to make the main point clearer
the text/message needs to be clearer, since the feedback says the meaning isn't clear even though the picture works
stepByStepSolution: Read the feedback carefully — the picture is liked, but the message is unclear.
This means the problem is with the words or overall message, not the picture.
The revision should focus on making the text clearer, so the poster's message is easy to understand.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all parts of the poster need to be changed, when the feedback only points to one part
Focusing on the picture, which the feedback says already works well
hints: Look carefully at exactly what the feedback says is unclear.
The feedback praises the picture, so focus elsewhere.

items.questionText: Which is the BEST reason to revise a multimodal text based on feedback, rather than ignoring it? A) Feedback is always right about everything.   B) Feedback can point out things the creator might not have noticed, helping the message become clearer for the audience.   C) You must always change everything a person suggests.
items.answerKey: Feedback can point out things the creator might not have noticed, helping the message become clearer for the audience.
stepByStepSolution: Think about why feedback is given in the first place — usually to help improve a piece of work.
A creator might not notice certain problems themselves, since they know their own intended message.
Listening carefully to feedback can help make the message clearer for the actual audience reading or viewing it.
commonMisconceptions: Believing all feedback must be followed exactly without thinking it through
Thinking feedback has no real value and can always be ignored
hints: Think about why someone else's point of view might notice something you missed.
The goal of revising is to make the message clearer, not to please everyone.

items.questionText: Explain the difference between revising a multimodal text's WORDS versus revising its IMAGES, and give an example of feedback that would lead to each type of change.
answerKey: revising words might mean fixing unclear sentences or a confusing message, like feedback saying 'the message isn't clear'; revising images might mean changing a picture that doesn't match the mood or topic, like feedback saying 'the picture doesn't match the story'

word changes fix the meaning or clarity of the text (e.g. feedback: 'I don't understand the message'), while image changes fix how the picture matches the topic or mood (e.g. feedback: 'the picture looks too happy for a scary story')
stepByStepSolution: Word revisions usually respond to feedback about unclear meaning or confusing sentences.
Image revisions usually respond to feedback about a picture not matching the topic or mood.
Recognising which type of feedback you received helps you know whether to revise the words or the images.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any feedback means changing everything, both words and images, instead of targeting the right part
Confusing feedback about clarity of meaning with feedback about visual mood
hints: Think about what kind of problem feedback about 'confusing message' points to.
Think about what kind of problem feedback about 'doesn't match the mood' points to.

items.questionText: A book trailer's music sounds cheerful and upbeat, but the trailer shows a sad, emotional scene. What feedback would be most useful to give? A) The colours in the trailer are wrong.   B) The music doesn't match the mood of the scene shown.   C) The trailer is too long.
items.answerKey: The music doesn't match the mood of the scene shown.
stepByStepSolution: In a multimodal text like a video, sound and images should work together to create one mood.
Here, cheerful music clashes with a sad, emotional scene, creating a mismatch.
The most useful feedback points directly at this mismatch between music and mood.
commonMisconceptions: Giving feedback about an unrelated feature, like colour or length, instead of the actual mismatch
Not noticing that music is also part of a multimodal text, alongside images
hints: Think about which two elements in the trailer don't match each other.
The clash is between the sound and the feeling of the scene.

items.questionText: Why might a creator ask other people for feedback on their poster or video before finishing it? A) To find out what other people would change or improve about their work   B) To make the project take longer for no reason   C) Feedback is not useful for improving multimodal texts
items.answerKey: To find out what other people would change or improve about their work
stepByStepSolution: Getting feedback means finding out how a piece of work looks or feels to someone else.
Other people can notice problems or ideas the creator may not have thought of.
This helps the creator improve their poster or video before it is finished.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking feedback is only useful after a project is completely finished
Believing feedback has no real purpose in improving multimodal work
hints: Think about what feedback actually helps someone do.
It helps the creator see their work from someone else's point of view.

items.questionText: A text is written to make readers laugh, using silly jokes and funny characters. What is this text's main purpose? A) To inform   B) To persuade   C) To entertain
items.answerKey: To entertain
stepByStepSolution: Look at the features described — silly jokes and funny characters.
These features are designed to make readers laugh and enjoy themselves.
This shows the text's main purpose is to entertain.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing entertaining features, like jokes, with persuasive techniques
Assuming any text with characters must be meant to inform
hints: Think about what jokes and funny characters are usually meant to do.
This purpose is about enjoyment, not facts or opinions.

items.questionText: A pamphlet uses facts, diagrams and clear headings to explain how volcanoes form. What is its main purpose? A) To entertain   B) To inform   C) To persuade
items.answerKey: To inform
stepByStepSolution: Look at the features described — facts, diagrams and clear headings.
These features are typically used to explain and teach the reader something.
This shows the text's main purpose is to inform.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing informative diagrams with persuasive images
Assuming any text about an interesting topic like volcanoes must be meant to entertain
hints: Think about what facts and diagrams are usually used for.
This purpose is about teaching the reader something true.

items.questionText: A persuasive text about eating more vegetables uses only boring, complicated facts and no emotive language or rhetorical questions. Is this text likely to be very effective at persuading children? Explain your answer.
answerKey: no, because it does not use techniques like emotive language or rhetorical questions that would appeal to children and convince them
it is probably not very effective, since persuasive texts usually need engaging techniques, and boring facts alone may not convince or interest child readers
stepByStepSolution: Think about what makes persuasive writing effective, especially for children.
Persuasive techniques like emotive language and rhetorical questions help engage and convince readers.
Without these techniques, and with only boring facts, the text is unlikely to be very effective at persuading children.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any true facts are automatically persuasive, regardless of how they are presented
Not considering the specific audience (children) when judging effectiveness
hints: Think about what usually makes persuasive writing convincing and engaging.
Consider whether boring, complicated facts alone would interest young readers.

items.questionText: A story for Year 3 students uses long, complicated words and very few pictures. How effectively does this suit its audience? A) Very effectively, because Year 3 students love difficult words.   B) Not very effectively, because Year 3 students usually need simpler language and visual support.   C) It doesn't matter at all for a story's effectiveness.
items.answerKey: Not very effectively, because Year 3 students usually need simpler language and visual support.
stepByStepSolution: Think about the reading level and needs of Year 3 students.
Year 3 students generally benefit from simpler language and helpful pictures.
A story using complicated words and few pictures is not well suited to this audience, making it less effective.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming harder vocabulary always makes a text better, regardless of audience
Believing audience needs don't matter when judging how effective a text is
hints: Think about what Year 3 readers typically find helpful in a story.
Consider both the vocabulary and the amount of pictures.

items.questionText: What question should you ask yourself to evaluate whether an informative text has achieved its purpose?
answerKey: does this text clearly teach me something true and useful about the topic
did I learn accurate, clear information from this text
stepByStepSolution: An informative text's purpose is to teach the reader true, useful information.
To evaluate its effectiveness, ask whether it clearly explained the topic and taught you something.
If the text achieves this clearly, it has been effective at its purpose of informing.
commonMisconceptions: Asking whether the text was entertaining, which is a different purpose from informing
Focusing only on the text's length rather than whether it taught anything clearly
hints: Think about what an informative text is supposed to do for the reader.
Your question should be about learning something, not about enjoyment.

items.questionText: A persuasive letter about protecting the environment includes strong emotive language and rhetorical questions but has several confusing, poorly organised sentences. How effective is this letter likely to be? A) Completely effective, because emotive language alone always works.   B) Only partly effective, because confusing sentences could stop the reader from following or being convinced by the argument.   C) Completely ineffective, because persuasive devices never work in any text.
items.answerKey: Only partly effective, because confusing sentences could stop the reader from following or being convinced by the argument.
stepByStepSolution: Think about what is needed for a persuasive text to work well — both good techniques AND clear writing.
This letter has good persuasive techniques but poor sentence organisation.
Because the confusing sentences might stop readers from following the argument, the letter is likely only partly effective, not completely effective or completely ineffective.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming persuasive devices alone guarantee full effectiveness, ignoring clarity
Assuming persuasive devices never work just because part of the text has a flaw
hints: Think about what happens if a reader gets confused partway through an argument.
Good techniques alone aren't always enough if the writing is unclear.

items.questionText: A funny story for young children uses very complicated, advanced humour that adults would understand but children would not. Explain why this makes the story less effective for its intended audience.
answerKey: because the audience (children) won't understand or enjoy the humour, so the story fails to entertain the people it was meant for
the story is meant to entertain children, but if the jokes are too advanced for them to understand, it won't achieve its purpose of making them laugh
stepByStepSolution: Think about who the story's intended audience actually is — young children.
If the humour is too advanced, children may not understand or find it funny.
Since the text's purpose is to entertain children specifically, humour they cannot understand makes the text less effective for that audience.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming any humour makes a story effective, regardless of whether the audience understands it
Confusing the needs of an adult audience with the needs of a child audience
hints: Think about who is actually meant to read and enjoy this story.
Effectiveness depends on whether THIS audience understands the humour.

items.questionText: Which is the BEST way to judge how effectively a text achieves its purpose? A) Check only if the text uses big, impressive words.   B) Check whether the text achieves what it set out to do (inform, persuade or entertain) for its intended audience.   C) Check only how long the text is.
items.answerKey: Check whether the text achieves what it set out to do (inform, persuade or entertain) for its intended audience.
stepByStepSolution: Evaluating effectiveness means checking if a text successfully does its job.
This means considering both its purpose (inform, persuade or entertain) and its intended audience.
Surface features like word difficulty or length do not, on their own, tell you whether a text is effective.
commonMisconceptions: Judging a text only by its vocabulary difficulty rather than its purpose and audience
Judging a text's effectiveness only by its length
hints: Think about what really matters: purpose AND audience together.
Length and difficult words alone don't determine effectiveness.

items.questionText: A weather report uses clear facts, simple graphs and short sentences to explain tomorrow's forecast. Based on its purpose, how effective is this text likely to be? A) Very effective, because it clearly and simply informs the reader.   B) Not effective, because it doesn't use any jokes.   C) Not effective, because it doesn't try to persuade anyone.
items.answerKey: Very effective, because it clearly and simply informs the reader.
stepByStepSolution: Identify the purpose of a weather report — to inform the reader clearly.
The report uses clear facts, simple graphs and short sentences, all of which support clear communication.
Since these features match the purpose of informing, the text is likely to be very effective.
commonMisconceptions: Expecting an informative text to also entertain or persuade, which are not its main purpose
Judging the report as ineffective simply because it lacks unrelated features like jokes or persuasion
hints: Think about what a weather report is actually trying to do.
Check if the features described match that purpose.

items.questionText: Name the three main purposes a text can have (hint: to teach, to convince, or to amuse).
answerKey: to inform, to persuade, and to entertain
inform, persuade, entertain
stepByStepSolution: Texts are usually written for one or more of three main purposes.
These purposes are to inform (teach), to persuade (convince) and to entertain (amuse).
Knowing these three purposes helps you evaluate how effectively any text achieves its goal.
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting one of the three purposes, such as leaving out 'entertain'
Confusing 'persuade' with 'inform', since both can use facts
hints: Think of three words: teach, convince, and amuse.
There are exactly three main purposes to remember.
